sections.h2: Which Osceola County office answers my tax question?
sections.html:
Three offices share the work, each with its own phone line, so it pays to pick the right one before you dial. The Property Appraiser sets assessed value and handles exemptions, tangible property returns and the tax roll; its main number is (407) 742-5000, and its site offers a tax estimator and a homestead filing page. The Tax Collector prints and mails the notices, takes payment and runs the tax certificate process. The clerk, who is also the county recorder, keeps the Official Records where deeds and mortgages are filed.

The Tax Collector answers at 407-742-4000 and operates four offices, all open weekdays until 4:00 pm: the main office at 2501 E. Irlo Bronson Memorial Hwy in Kissimmee, another at 2595 Simpson Road in Kissimmee, a St. Cloud office at 1300 9th Street, Suite 101B, and a Campbell City office at 4730 South Orange Blossom Trail. Appointments can be booked online.

  • Osceola County Property Appraiser: value, exemptions, millage page, tax estimator.
  • Osceola County Tax Collector: notices, payment, installment plan, certificates.
  • Osceola Clerk of Court and Comptroller: Official Records search, which includes a property fraud alert signup.

Collection for the January through December assessment year opens November 1. Notices normally go out by then to the last address on the tax roll, and payment runs through March, with April 1 as the delinquency date.

When a mortgage escrow pays the tax, the lender is supposed to request the bill and send you a copy. Even so, the Tax Collector reminds owners that making sure the tax is paid and a bill is received falls on the owner.

Dates an Osceola County owner should know
DateWhat happens
January 1Assessment and valuation date
March 1Deadline to file for exemptions
March 31Gross amount due on real estate tax
April 1Unpaid real estate tax delinquent, 3 percent charge added; tangible personal property returns due
April 30Installment plan applications for next year due

sections.h2: Early discounts and the installment plan
sections.html:
Pay in November and the bill drops by 4 percent. The break loses a point each month, down to 1 percent in February, and March payers owe the gross amount.

The installment plan splits the year into four payments. Applications for the following year are due April 30, and the first payment is owed by June 30. Paying it in July forfeits the discount and adds a 5 percent late charge, and missing July 31 cancels the plan. Two more payments follow, on September 30 and December 31.

A separate tangible personal property bill covers furniture, fixtures and equipment in businesses and rentals, plus structural additions to mobile homes. Estimated tax over $100.00 may be paid quarterly. A landlord selling a furnished rental should ask the appraiser about the April 1 return.

  • Discounts apply to both real estate and tangible personal property bills.
  • Name, address and assessed value changes go through the Property Appraiser, not the Tax Collector.

sections.h2: Homestead for a seller or buyer
sections.html:
File with the Property Appraiser by March 1; the benefit starts with the year you file. The homestead benefit is capped at $50,000 in two tiers, and only the first reaches school taxes.

The appraiser's site has a File Homestead page and a form for reporting exemption fraud, and the clerk offers a property fraud alert. When you sell, let the appraiser know. A sale or deed ends the capped assessment, and the value resets at the next January 1. A buyer who plans to live in the house files a new application by the March deadline.

Farmland holds its own classification, and Osceola's appraiser says that classification does not pass to a new owner. Someone buying pasture or grove land applies again in the January to March window, and classified parcels are re-inspected at least every three years.

The sequence is fixed. On April 1 the unpaid tax gets a 3 percent charge, the parcel is advertised, a lien is sold, and after two years the certificate holder can apply for a tax deed.

The delinquent list runs in parcel order in a local paper for three straight weeks. By the first of June, the collector holds a public online auction on LienHub. Bidding opens at 18 percent, and the certificate goes to the investor who accepts the lowest rate. A certificate is a lien, not a deed, and it gives the buyer no right to enter your property.

To clear it, pay the certificate amount plus interest at the rate it sold for, and add a $6.25 redemption fee on or after June 1. Certificates no investor wanted are sold later through LienHub. If a certificate is still open on the second April 1 after the sale, the holder may ask for a tax deed, after paying off other certificates on the parcel and the current year's tax.

  • For the first two years, a certificate holder may not press you for payment.
  • You can sell with a lien in place; closing pays it off.

sections.h2: Taxes and the deed at closing
sections.html:
The tax lien is paid at the closing table, and then the deed goes into the Official Records. Florida's stamp tax on the deed is 70 cents for each $100 of the price, with Miami-Dade the one exception. Every signer of the deed answers for it, and the clerk collects it at recording.

State law also sets a per-page recording charge, with a modernization trust fund charge and a technology charge added. Osceola's clerk has opened a Poinciana branch office as well.

Timing matters. Bills mail in November, so a closing before then leaves the new year's bill unissued. Ask your closing agent how the year will be prorated, and keep the Tax Collector's payoff letter in your closing file. If a 10 percent non-homestead cap applied to your rental, expect the buyer's value to reset after the sale.

sections.h2: What a seller can do this month
sections.html:
Pull up the parcel on the appraiser's site and confirm the owner name and any exemption are right. Then look at the Tax Collector's account for the same parcel and note which years are paid. If there is a balance, phone 407-742-4000 and ask for the payoff in writing. Finally, put the payoff letter, your latest notice and a copy of the deed into one folder for the title agent.

Choosing between a regular listing and a cash sale does not change any of this. The tax lien rides with the parcel either way, and closing pays it from the proceeds.

faqs.q: What is the delinquency date for Osceola County tax?
faqs.a: April 1. The Tax Collector adds a 3 percent charge to the gross amount that day, advertises the delinquent list, and runs an online lien auction by June 1.

faqs.q: What discounts does the Osceola County Tax Collector give?
faqs.a: Four percent off for November, then a point less each month through February. March brings no discount, and March 31 is the gross due date.

faqs.q: Where is the Osceola County Tax Collector?
faqs.a: The main office is at 2501 E. Irlo Bronson Memorial Hwy in Kissimmee. Others sit on Simpson Road in Kissimmee, in St. Cloud and in Campbell City, all on the 407-742-4000 line.

faqs.q: How do I redeem an Osceola County tax certificate?
faqs.a: Pay the certificate amount plus interest at the rate it sold for, and a $6.25 fee when redeeming on or after June 1. Contact the Tax Collector for the exact payoff.

faqs.q: Does back tax stop me from selling in Osceola County?
faqs.a: No. The lien rides with the parcel and the payoff is deducted at closing. Before you sign, phone 407-742-4000 and ask the Tax Collector for the number.
